title: Screen time: knowing when to switch off
keyIdea: Screens are fine for a short time, but a growing body also needs to move, play, talk and sleep. Ask a grown-up before you use a phone, tablet or TV. When the timer rings, the show ends or a grown-up says stop, switch it off yourself, instead of asking for one more, hiding it or carrying on. Keep screens off at meals, so everyone can talk, and in the hour before bed, because screens keep the brain awake and sleep comes late. After a show, run, jump or play. Feeling cross when it goes off is normal: take a big breath, say bye to the screen and choose what to do next.
familyTip: Before a show, set a kitchen timer together and agree what happens when it rings. Let your child press the off button and pick the next thing: a run outside, a book or a game with you. Keep phones off the dinner table and out of the bedroom, and do the same yourself, because children copy what they see.

visual.caption: Screen on or screen off? Drag each card into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: switch off when the timer rings, make a screen-free bedtime, turn off screens at dinner, plan a day and calm the cross feeling.

kid: Screens are fun. A show or a game is OK for a short time. But your body also needs to run, play, talk and sleep. Ask a grown-up before you use a phone, a tablet or the TV.
When the timer rings, switch it off. When the show ends, switch it off. When a grown-up says stop, switch it off. Do not ask for one more. Do not hide it. You can press the off button yourself.
Screens go off at meals. Then we can eat and talk. Screens go off before bed too. A screen keeps your brain awake, so sleep comes late. Have a bath, brush your teeth and read a story instead.
It is OK to feel cross when the screen goes off. Take a big breath. Say, “Bye, TV!” Then choose what to do next, like a game of ball or a book. The cross feeling gets smaller.
adult: Ages 4 to 5. DfE Development Matters (2021) asks Reception children to 'know and talk about the different factors that support their overall health and wellbeing', naming 'sensible amounts of screen time' and 'having a good sleep routine'. This is also part of the EYFS Early Learning Goal Managing Self. Key words: screen, timer, switch off, bedtime, mealtime, cross, calm.

How much: the WHO (2019) guidelines for children under 5 say that for ages 3 to 4, sitting at screens should be no more than 1 hour a day, and less is better. The UK RCPCH (2019) gives no fixed limit but advises no screens in the hour before bed, and asks families to agree a plan. The AAP (2016) suggests screen-free meals and bedrooms, and watching together when you can.

Common mistakes: asking for 'one more' every time; hiding the tablet or turning the sound down to keep watching; thinking a screen in bed helps them get sleepy, when it pushes sleep later; screens left on at the table; and treating anger at switch-off as naughtiness. Strong feelings at a transition are normal at this age. Warn before the end, stop at the end of a show, and offer a next activity.

The lab has a child switch off at three different signals, choose calm things for bedtime, tap the screens off at dinner, place two short shows in a day (never at meals or bedtime), and pick calming steps when the cross feeling comes. Children copy adults, so your own screen habits matter as much as the rules.

practice.prompt: Screen time: the timer rings while you watch a show. What do you do?
choices: Hide the tablet under a cushion
practice.hint: The timer is the signal we agreed on.
practice.explain: When the timer rings, it is time to stop, so you switch it off. One more show or hiding it means the screen is still on.

practice.prompt: At dinner, {n} screens are on. You switch off 2 of them. How many are still on?
practice.hint: Hold up {n} fingers, then fold down 2 for the screens you switched off.
practice.explain: {n} take away 2 leaves {=n-2} screens still on. Switch those off too, so everyone can talk and eat.

practice.prompt: You read {a} books at bedtime, then {b} more. How many books is that?
practice.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more, one for each book.
practice.explain: {a} books and {b} more books make {=a+b} books. Books, not screens, help you get sleepy.

practice.prompt: Is a tablet game in bed good for sleep?
choices: No, it keeps your brain awake
Yes, if the sound is off
practice.hint: Does a game make your brain busy or calm?
practice.explain: Screens keep your brain busy and awake, so sleep comes late. Screens go off in the hour before bed.

practice.prompt: The TV goes off and you feel cross. What helps?
practice.hint: Which one helps the cross feeling get smaller?
practice.explain: A big breath helps you calm down. Throwing can break things, and switching it back on breaks the rule.

pool.prompt: You want to use Mum's phone. What do you do first?
pool.hint: Who does the phone belong to?
pool.explain: Phones and tablets belong to grown-ups, so you always ask a grown-up first.

pool.prompt: Where do screens go at dinner time?
choices: Off, so we can talk and eat
On the table, so I can watch
pool.hint: What do families do together at the table?
pool.explain: At meals, screens are off. Then everyone can eat, talk and listen to each other.

pool.prompt: You watched a show. What is good to do next?
pool.hint: Your body sat still for the show.
pool.explain: After sitting at a screen, your body needs to move. Running and playing help you grow strong.

pool.prompt: When is a good time for a short show?
pool.hint: Screens are off at meals and before bed.
pool.explain: A short show in the afternoon is fine. Dinner and bedtime are screen-off times.

pool.prompt: Dad says, “Time to stop.” The show has 1 minute left. What is fair?
choices: Finish the show, then switch off
pool.hint: Stopping at the end of a show is easier.
pool.explain: Finishing the last minute and then switching off is fair. Starting a new show or pretending not to hear is not stopping.

pool.prompt: You have {n} turns on the slide after your show. Then you have 1 more. How many turns is that?
pool.hint: Start at {n} and count on 1 more turn on the slide.
pool.explain: {n} turns and 1 more make {=n+1} turns. Moving after a show is good for your body.

pool.prompt: There are {n} screens on. You switch 1 off. How many are still on?
pool.hint: Hold up {n} fingers, then fold down 1 for the screen you switched off.
pool.explain: {n} take away 1 leaves {=n-1} screens on. Keep going until they are all off.

pool.prompt: Why do screens go off before bed?
choices: They make the room too cold
pool.explain: Screens keep the brain busy and awake, so sleep comes late. A bath, teeth and a story help you get sleepy.

pool.prompt: You feel cross when the tablet goes off. Is that OK?
choices: Yes, and a big breath helps
No, you must never feel cross
Yes, so you can shout and kick
pool.hint: Feelings are OK. What we do with them matters.
pool.explain: Feeling cross is normal. Take a big breath, say bye to the screen and choose what to do next.
